title: Apple launches $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs, its first paid AI tier
subtitle: The one-time top-up adds AI usage inside Logic Pro's Creator Studio once a monthly limit is hit — a narrow start to what Apple calls a future broader paid tier.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Apple launched Intelligence Usage Packs on November 9, a one-time $49.99 top-up that adds AI usage to Logic Pro's Creator Studio features after a user burns through the included monthly limit. The pack is purchased from inside Logic Pro via Intelligence Features → Show Usage → Buy More Usage. Availability is narrow — eight countries at launch, including the US, UK, and Canada, with most of Europe and most of Asia excluded. Unused usage rolls over month to month and expires 12 months after purchase, and the packs do not support Family Sharing. Apple has not disclosed how many AI operations the $49.99 pack actually buys.

This is the first time Apple has charged any consumer directly for AI usage, and the design is deliberately conservative. Instead of a subscription — which locks users into recurring billing and is the model OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft have all converged on — Apple shipped a one-time top-up tied to a single app. It is a usage pack, not a plan, and it only matters to the subset of Logic Pro subscribers who are heavy enough users of the AI features to hit the monthly ceiling. Apple had foreshadowed this in an iOS 27 footnote that said expanded Apple Intelligence access would require a fee, without naming a date or price, so the launch delivers on that promise without committing to the broader subscription model the footnote hinted at.

The strategic read is that Apple is testing willingness-to-pay inside a professional product before touching the consumer-facing Apple Intelligence surface area. Logic Pro's user base skews toward prosumers and small studios — people who already pay for a Mac, already pay for Logic, and are plausibly willing to pay for AI that shortens a production workflow. If the $49.99 pack sells, Apple has a pricing anchor and a usage baseline for Final Cut, Keyboard dictation, Image Playground, and the broader Intelligence stack. If it does not, Apple learns that at a low cost. Compare this to Microsoft's Copilot bundling, which forced a per-seat decision on the entire enterprise in one move, and the Apple approach reads as cautious by design.

A takeaway for learners: pricing is a product decision, not a finance decision. The mechanism Apple chose — one-time top-ups, inside the app, with rollover — sends a specific signal: we think AI usage is bursty, not continuous, and we want to see what you actually consume before we quote you a subscription. If you are shipping an AI product, think hard about which pricing shape fits how your users actually work. Flat subscriptions, usage-based, credits, and one-time packs each select for a different customer, and the wrong choice is the single easiest way to leave real revenue on the table.
